extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. It contains 16,000 questions, each paired with a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the article title, and a yes/no answer, and is intended to study the difficulty of answering natural yes/no questions that often require inference.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark; Kenton Lee; Ming-Wei Chang; Tom Kwiatkowski; Michael Collins; Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, and Kristina Toutanova. 2019. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was gathered using the Natural Questions pipeline with an additional filtering step for yes/no questions: questions were taken from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries, heuristically filtered for likely yes/no questions, kept only when a Wikipedia page appeared in the first five search results, and then paired with a Wikipedia article for human annotator processing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators could mark questions as "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine; Wikipedia pages returned among the first five search results; an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine; question/article pairs are given to a human annotator, who in a three-step process decides if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information), finds a passage within the Wikipedia document that contains enough information to answer the question or marks it not answerable, and finally marks whether the question’s answer is yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess annotation quality, three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples; when there was disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement as gold-standard labels, and the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to these gold-standard labels; because agreement was sufficiently high, the dataset uses singly-annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results; questions are only kept if annotators judge them to be comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information; the dataset uses singly-annotated examples and answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels; six disagreements were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage; “Yes” answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Naturally occurring yes/no questions have the benefit of being directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions; using naturally occurring questions avoids models optimized to perform in an artificial setting and ties the dataset to a clear end-task
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: to test models on their ability to answer naturally occurring yes/no questions; to construct highly inferential reading comprehension datasets; to test inferential abilities in reading comprehension; directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions are heuristically filtered to likely yes/no queries by selecting queries whose first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length; questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results; the dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set, and splits them into dev, test, and train sets with Natural Questions examples always in the train set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We only use questions that were marked as having a yes/no answer, and pair each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document; annotators can mark questions as not answerable, and only good questions that are comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information are kept.
